outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of the text:

---

Mother, the root of this little yellow flower
Among the stones bears the bitter taste of quinine.
How strange the cliff appears today. The sun shines so radiantly,
And the grasshopper labours at his sewing-machine
So diligently. Here's one upon my hand, mother, look;
I lie so perfectly still. There's another resting on your book.

But I have something stranger still to tell. So set aside
Your book for the grasshopper, mother dear,—
Like a green knight within a dazzling market-place,—
And listen now. Can you hear what I hear
Far out to sea? Now and then the foam there curls
And reaches out a white arm, slender as a girl's.

Fishes and gulls ring no bells. There surely cannot be
A chapel or a church between this place and Devon,
With fishes or gulls tolling its bell,—hark!—
Somewhere beneath the sea, or high in heaven.
"It's the bell, my son, far out within the bay,
Upon the buoy. It does ring sweetly today."

Sweeter I never heard, mother, no, not in all of Wales.
I should dearly love to lie beneath that foam,
Dead, yet still able to hear the sounding of the bell,
And certain that you would often come
To rest awhile, listening in quiet happiness.
I should be content, if only that could be.

---

outputs.L2:
Mother, this small yellow flower growing here
Between the rocks—its root tastes just like quinine.
Everything feels peculiar on the cliff today. The sunlight blazes,
And the grasshopper labors away at his sewing-machine
With such effort. See, mother, one has landed on my hand;
I stay so motionless. Another rests upon your book.
Yet I've something even stranger to share. So set
Your book aside for the grasshopper, dear mother—
He's like a green knight standing in a glittering marketplace—
And pay attention now. Do you catch what I catch
From far away? Every so often the foam out there twists
And reaches out a pale arm, just as a girl might do.
No bells are rung by fish or seagulls. Surely there's no
Chapel or church standing anywhere from here to Devon,
Where fish or gulls would toll a bell—just listen!—
Someplace beneath the waves or high above in heaven.
"That's the bell, my son, floating out in the bay
Upon the buoy. Today its ringing sounds so lovely."
I've never heard one lovelier, mother—not once, not anywhere in Wales.
How I'd love to rest beneath that foam,
Lifeless, yet still able to catch the bell's ringing,
And knowing for certain you would often visit
And sit here, listening with joy.
I would be content if only that were possible.

# On the Cliff

Sitting high upon the cliff, I take in the vivid details of the natural world around me. I pluck a small yellow flower and taste its bitterness on my tongue, while grasshoppers leap and land lightly upon my hand and across the pages of my mother's book. These small, immediate sensations ground me in the present moment, alive with color and movement.

Then, from far out at sea, I become aware of a strange and distant sound—a soft, bell-like ringing that seems to drift across the water toward me. It is mysterious and otherworldly, and I cannot help but wonder about its source. Could it be something supernatural, some voice from beyond the ordinary world calling out across the waves?

My mother, ever practical, offers a simple explanation. The sound, she tells me, is nothing more than a bell mounted upon a buoy, floating gently in the bay. There is nothing mysterious about it at all; it is an everyday object, marking the water for those who pass by.

Yet even knowing this, I find myself drawn to a haunting and melancholy wish. I imagine lying dead beneath the white foam of the sea, at peace beneath the waves, and yet somehow still able to hear that beautiful, distant bell ringing above me. There is a strange comfort in the thought—to rest forever while that lovely sound continues on.

Above all, my deepest desire is that my mother might one day come to visit me there. I long for her to rest peacefully near the place where I lie, to sit quietly beside my resting place. That, more than anything, would bring me happiness—the thought of her presence remaining close to me, even in death.
outputs.L4:
# The Bell Beneath the Sea

The boy lay stretched upon the sun-warmed grass at the cliff's edge, his small body pressed into the earth where wildflowers nodded in the breeze. All around him the world hummed with the languid warmth of a summer afternoon. Yellow blossoms trembled beside his cheek, releasing their faint sweetness into the air, while the sunlight fell golden and generous across the meadow, so bright it seemed to soak into his very skin.

Nearby, a grasshopper leapt through the tall stems, its papery wings clicking as it went. The boy watched it with half-closed eyes, following its restless motion, listening to the drowsy song of countless insects rising from the grass. Everything felt suspended in that moment—the light, the fragrance, the small living sounds—as though the world had paused simply to be beautiful.

"Mother," he said, turning his head to where she sat beside him, "do you hear it?"

She looked at him, uncertain.

"That sound," he continued, his voice soft with wonder. "There, coming from the sea. Like a bell ringing, far down beneath the waves." He pointed toward the water below, where the tide rolled and broke against the rocks, throwing up its white foam. "Can you hear it, Mother? A bell, tolling somewhere under the water."

She listened, but perhaps she heard nothing—only the ordinary murmur of the sea. Yet the child's face was rapt, tender, already half-elsewhere.

Then he spoke again, and his words carried a strange and quiet weight, far too heavy for one so young.

"Mother, I think I should like to lie down there—down beneath the foam, at the bottom of the sea. I should lie very still, and I would not be afraid. And even then I should still hear the bell ringing, sweet and clear through all the water above me."

His mother's heart caught, but the boy went on, smiling faintly, as if he described some gentle happiness.

"And you would come, wouldn't you? You would come to the edge of the cliff, just here, and you would listen too. You would hear the bell and be glad. And I would know that you were there, listening happily, and so I would be at peace."

There was no fear in him, only a serene and aching longing—a wish for the stillness of death made bearable, even beautiful, by the thought that his mother would remain close, listening to the same sweet sound. In his imagining, dying was not a separation but a quiet resting, a place where the bell would ring forever and where his mother's presence would keep watch above him, glad and unafraid.

And so the child lay in the sunlight among the flowers and the grasshoppers, alive and warm, yet dreaming tenderly of the cool foam below—of a peace that mingled death and love into one gentle, unbroken note, like a bell that never ceases ringing beneath the sea.

# The Things a Mother Keeps

There is a particular kind of magic in the things a mother holds onto. Long after her children have grown and scattered across the world, she remains the quiet keeper of small treasures—the crayon drawings, the first lost tooth wrapped in tissue, the tiny shoes that once carried unsteady steps across a kitchen floor.

The mother sees value where others see clutter. To her, a faded ticket stub is not paper but a memory of a summer afternoon. A chipped mug is not something to throw away but a reminder of mornings shared, of coffee and conversation, of the ordinary moments that turned out to be the important ones all along.

We often overlook these things when we are young. We hurry past them, eager to build our own lives, certain that the future holds everything that matters. But the mother knows a secret truth: the things we carry with us are rarely the grand or expensive ones. They are the small, worn, well-loved objects that speak of belonging.

Perhaps this is the deepest lesson a mother teaches—not through words, but through the gentle act of keeping. She reminds us that love is often found in the details, in the things we choose to hold close, and in the quiet hope that one day, we too will understand what was worth saving all along.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a sick child talking to his mother while lying on a cliff by the sea, mentioning a yellow flower, a grasshopper, and a bell ringing from a buoy in the bay.
counterfactuals.output:
**By the Sea, in June**

Mother, don't hold me quite so tight—
lay me down where the grass grows thin,
here on the cliff, in the falling light,
and let the small wind in.

Do you see that yellow flower, close by my hand?
It grew from a crack where nothing should grow.
I am too tired to reach it, but I understand
why it turns its face the way it does, so slow.

A grasshopper landed just now on my knee.
He weighs no more than a breath, than a thought.
He looked at me, Mother—he truly looked at me—
then leapt away like something I never caught.

Listen. The buoy is ringing out in the bay,
a bell that no one rings but the moving sea.
It says the same word over, all night, all day,
the way you say my name so quietly.

Don't cry. I only want to lie here and hear it,
the flower, the grasshopper, the bell, and you.
I am not afraid. I feel the whole world near it—
the cliff, the light, the ringing coming through.

Stay a little longer. The tide is low.
Tell me the names of things while I can hear.
I'll close my eyes, but I won't really go—
I'll be the flower. I'll be the bell. I'm here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue where a dying boy tells his mother he wishes to lie beneath the sea foam, still able to hear a church-like bell so she can visit him.
counterfactuals.output:
**Beneath the Foam**

Mother—no, do not weep yet. Come closer.
Set the candle down; the light hurts less
when your face is near it. There. Now sit.

I have been thinking, in these long hours,
of where they'll lay me down. Not in the churchyard—
please, not there, beneath the stones and rooks,
where the earth is cold and the winter locks it hard.
I could not bear the dark of it, Mother.
I could not bear to be so *still*.

Listen. You know the cove below the cliffs,
where the white foam curls and never sleeps?
That is where I'd lie. Not drowned—no, resting.
Cradled in the tide's soft rising, falling,
the sea-froth blooming over me like flowers,
cool and clean, forever moving.
I should not be alone there. The water speaks all night.

But Mother, I have one more asking of you.
There is a bell—the old one, in the chapel by the shore—
the one that rings when the fishing boats come home.
Hang it there. Let it swing above the water,
so when the wind comes off the waves
it tolls, and tolls, low as a heartbeat.

Then I shall hear it. Even sleeping.
Even fathoms down beneath the foam,
I'll know the sound and think: *she has not forgotten.*
And when you cannot find the strength to speak my name,
you'll come, and stand upon the cliff,
and hear it, too—and we will be together
in that ringing, you above and I below,
the sea between us thin as morning.

Do not cry, Mother. I am not afraid.
I am only going where the bell can reach me.
Ring it soft. Ring it slow.
And I will listen.
I will always listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholy free-verse poem set on the Welsh coast, with a child noticing quinine-tasting flowers and imagining bells ringing under the sea or in heaven.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bitter Flowers at Aberdaron**

The tide has gone out further than the day,
leaving the flat grey mirror of itself
where the child stands, small against so much sky,
and tastes the yellow flowers on the cliff—

quinine, she thinks, though she has no word for it,
only the pucker, the sudden wince,
the way the bitterness lives at the back of the tongue
like something remembered before she was born.

The gorse says nothing. The sheep say nothing.
The wind comes up from the water with its cold mouth
and the whole coast leans, the way a mother leans
over a cradle she is about to leave.

She listens. She is always listening now.
Somewhere below the green shelf of the sea
there are bells, she is certain, bronze and drowned,
churches that slid under a hundred winters ago,

still ringing, patient, for a village that forgot them—
or else the sound is coming down from heaven,
which she pictures as another kind of water,
paler, and warmer, and with no far shore.

She cannot tell which. Perhaps it is the same.
Perhaps the bells beneath and the bells above
are the one bell, and she is standing between them
holding a flower too bitter to be swallowed,

her cardigan the colour of the last light,
her name already half-taken by the wind.
The tide will turn. The bells will go on ringing.
No one will come to tell her it is time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an early 20th-century English pastoral poem about a mother and son on a cliff, blending nature imagery with the child's thoughts of death and longing.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cliff-Edge

Upon the chalk-white brow of Beachy Head
My mother walks; the grasses at her feet
Are bent with dew, and overhead
The larks dissolve in light. So sweet
The morning breaks, so mild the air,
And yet I think of graves, and those laid there.

She does not know. She points to where the gulls
Wheel white above the fretting of the tide,
To distant sails, to weathered hulls,
To all the living world and wide—
While I, who am but seven years,
Feel in my breast the pricking start of tears.

For everything so beautiful must die.
The clover-heads, the poppies' scarlet flame,
The very swifts that thread the sky
Will pass, as all things pass, the same
As she must pass, my mother dear,
Who takes my hand and does not see my fear.

I long to tell her: *When you go from me,
Let me go too, beneath the same green sod;
Bury me by the sounding sea,
And let us keep our tryst with God
Together, hand in warm-held hand*—
But cannot speak, nor will she understand.

The wind comes off the Channel, cool and long,
And lifts the ribbons of her Sunday dress.
She sings a half-remembered song.
I press against her, wordless, press
My cheek to where her heart's slow beat
Sounds like the sea below us, grave and sweet.

O let this moment stand outside of time,
The gulls held fast, the tide forever full,
The larks arrested in their climb,
And I forever at her side, and small—
Before the years divide us, and the deep
Chalk earth receives us into separate sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
